evidence: Disassembly is unambiguous about the mechanism: it compares a byte fetched through the pointer returned by FUN_00056799 against the standard IBM PC scancode set (0x48/0x50/0x4B/0x4D arrows, 0x1C Enter, 0x39 Space, 0x01 Esc), adjusts the globals 0x00069cd4 / 0x00069ccc in steps of 0x18 with bounds derived from the map dimension shorts at 0x00060144 scaled by 0x18, scrolls the separate origin pair 0x00069ce0 / 0x00069ce4 to keep the cursor within a 0x108 by 0x90 pixel window, and calls the already-named fdps_map_cursor_move_to and fdps_render_view_frame. The 0x50-byte stride from base 0x00069cd8 with count 0x00060150 is the unit array, so the candidate list holds unit indices. Callers include fdps_battle_unit_turn, which places it in the battle subsystem, hence the fdps_ prefix. Calling convention: the prologue pushes EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP and reads all three arguments from [EBP+0x14], [EBP+0x18] and [EBP+0x1c] without touching EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX on entry, and the function ends in a plain RET, so the arguments arrive on the stack and the caller cleans up. The string constant pushed to FUN_0002a1f0 is "Beep.wav" at 0x00061e78, confirming that call is the cursor-move sound effect.
open_question: The exact meaning of the mode values 4, 5 and 6 is not settled (mode 6 clearly means 'the acting unit is selecting a destination or target and the list argument carries its own index'), and the semantics of FUN_0002ba00's outputs 0x00069d09 / 0x00069d0c (tile cost table pointer and resolved occupant index) are inferred from use rather than read.

name: fdps_map_load_tile_info
role: Reads the map cell at column x, row y out of the loaded map layers and caches the terrain tile id, its four attribute bytes and two auxiliary per-cell bytes into a fixed block of globals that the rest of the battle code then inspects.
plate_comment:
Loads the per-cell map information for one battle map tile into the shared "current tile" globals.

Algorithm:
1. Reads the terrain layer pointer at 0x00069cb0. The layer header stores the map width as a 16-bit value at offset 7 and the cell array (one 16-bit tile id per cell) starts at offset 0xb. The linear cell index is y * width + x; the tile id read from that slot is stored to the global at 0x00069d04.
2. Uses that tile id to index the tile attribute table pointed to by 0x00069c98: entries are 4 bytes each and begin at offset 0x11 of the table. The four bytes of the entry are copied out individually, in the order byte2 -> 0x00069d09, byte0 -> 0x00069d08, byte1 -> 0x00069d0a, byte3 -> 0x00069d0b.
3. Indexes a second layer pointed to by 0x00060144 with the same linear cell index (2 bytes per cell, array at offset 4) and copies the high byte of that cell to the global at 0x00069d0c.
4. Indexes a third layer pointed to by 0x00060148, whose own width field lives at offset 7 of its header and whose cell array is one byte per cell starting at offset 0x10. The byte is zero-extended and stored to the 16-bit global at 0x00069d06.
The function performs no bounds checking on x or y and calls nothing.

Parameters:
  x - map column index, pushed last by the caller.
  y - map row index.

Returns:
  Nothing. All results are delivered through the globals at 0x00069d04, 0x00069d06, 0x00069d08, 0x00069d09, 0x00069d0a, 0x00069d0b and 0x00069d0c.
evidence: Disassembly computes y * (*(short *)(layer + 7)) + x twice over two different layer base pointers and once more over a third layer with its own width field, which is the signature shape of a tile lookup on a width-major 2D map. Element strides (2 bytes for the two 16-bit layers, 1 byte for the third, 4 bytes for the attribute table indexed by the tile id just read) and the fixed header offsets 0xb / 0x11 / 4 / 0x10 all match container layouts with a small header followed by a cell array. Every result is written to a contiguous group of globals at 0x00069d04..0x00069d0c rather than returned, i.e. a shared "current tile" record. It is a leaf (no callees) called from 15 distinct functions, one of which is already named fdps_battle_map_overview, so it is game logic in the battle map subsystem, not CRT or AIL. Calling convention is settled by the call site at 000108bf: two PUSH EAX followed by CALL and ADD ESP,0x8 (caller cleanup), matching the [EBP+0x14] / [EBP+0x18] stack parameter reads and the plain RET in the callee.
open_question: The meaning of the individual fields is not settled: which of the four attribute bytes is movement cost, defence bonus, avoid bonus or passability flag, and what the layers at 0x00060144 (high byte of a 16-bit cell) and 0x00060148 (single byte per cell) represent - candidates are the unit-occupancy layer and an event/zone layer. Resolving that needs a consumer of globals 0x00069d06..0x00069d0c to be read.

name: fdps_battle_player_phase_loop
role: Interactive battle-map loop for the player's phase: polls the keyboard, moves the map cursor and scrolls the camera on a 24-pixel tile grid, cycles to the next actionable friendly unit, and dispatches unit selection to the command menu, the unit-info screen or the battle menu until the phase-end flag is set.
plate_comment:
Player-phase interactive loop on the battle map.

Algorithm:
Obtains the shared keyboard-state byte via the low-level key accessor at 0x56799 and primes it to 0xFF. Reads the map dimensions from the header pointed to by 0x60144 (word 0 = width, word 1 = height) and converts both to pixel extents by multiplying by the 24-pixel tile size. Then loops until the local exit flag becomes non-zero.

Each iteration polls input (0x30c50), reads the current scancode and maintains an auto-repeat counter: the same scancode as last time increments the counter, a different one resets it and records the new code. An action is only taken when the counter is 0 (first press) or greater than 5 (auto-repeat has kicked in); F1 (0x3B) and F2/Home (0x3C/0x47) are handled on the suppressed path instead.

Scancode dispatch:
  0x48/0x50 (up/down)    move the cursor Y at 0x69CCC by one tile, clamped to the map height
  0x4B/0x4D (left/right) move the cursor X at 0x69CD4 by one tile, clamped to the map width
                         each accepted move calls the feedback routine at 0x2A1F0 with the descriptor at 0x61E78
  0x01/0x2C/0x4C/0x53    cycle forward through the unit table: starting from the saved rotation index,
                         scan up to unit-count (0x60150) entries of the 0x50-byte records based at 0x69CD8
                         and stop at the first with (flags[+5] & 0x85) == 0 and side[+6] == 2, then centre
                         on it via 0x2D7C0 with its tile coordinates scaled by 24, saving the next index
  0x1C/0x39 (Enter/Space) clear the key latch (0x567B3), resolve the unit under the cursor (0x2DAA0);
                         with no unit, open the battle menu (0x14AB0) and take its return as the exit flag;
                         with a unit that is friendly (side[+6] == 2), not marked done (flags[+5] & 0x80)
                         and with byte +0x26 clear, open the unit command menu (0x15470) and, if the
                         phase-end flag 0x69DA0 is still clear, run the post-command step (0x2EA10);
                         otherwise show the read-only unit info screen (0x16AA0)
  0x3B (F1)              invoke the routine at 0x2E160
  0x3C/0x47 (F2/Home)    resolve the unit under the cursor and show its info screen (0x16AA0)

After dispatch the camera origin (X at 0x69CE4, Y at 0x69CE0) is scrolled by one tile whenever the cursor comes within one tile of a viewport edge, clamped so the viewport (0x138 by 0xC0 pixels) stays inside the map. The frame is then drawn by 0x2BEB0, and the loop exits once the phase-end flag at 0x69DA0 is non-zero.

Parameters:
None. The decompiler's param_1/param_2/unaff_EBX are artifacts; no incoming stack slot or register is read before being written.

Returns:
Nothing.
evidence: The scancode constants 0x48/0x50/0x4B/0x4D (arrows), 0x1C (Enter), 0x39 (Space), 0x01 (Esc), 0x3B/0x3C (F1/F2), 0x47 (Home) identify it as a keyboard-driven interactive loop. All coordinate arithmetic is in units of 0x18 (24 px tile), map extents come from the two words at [0x60144], and the loop indexes 0x50-byte records based at 0x69CD8 with the count at 0x60150 and tests a side byte (+6 == 2) and a flags byte (+5 & 0x85 / & 0x80), which is the battle unit table. It is called from exactly one place, main at 0x29220, and it drives per-frame rendering (0x2BEB0) and menu/info entry points, so it is a top-level game-logic loop, not a runtime helper -- hence the fdps_ prefix and the battle subsystem. Calling convention: the prologue is the exact -4s stack-convention shape documented in rebuild_info/build_flags.md (PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP; MOV EBP,ESP; MOV ESP,EBP / POP on exit, no LEAVE), and every callee here is called with PUSH followed by ADD ESP,n at the call site, so the module default (__cdecl) applies. The function itself reads no argument slot, so it is void(void).
open_question: The exact meaning of unit-record bytes +5 (bit 0x80 'has acted', bits 0x05 unknown), +6 (side/faction, value 2 taken as the player's side) and +0x26 is inferred from the tests here only; the flag at 0x69DA0 is treated as 'phase or battle ended' but its writer was not examined. Whether 0x2A1F0 with the descriptor at 0x61E78 is a cursor-move sound effect or a redraw call is unresolved.

name: fdps_render_view_frame
role: Allocates an 86400-byte offscreen scene buffer, lets two helpers fill and decorate it, then presents a 312x192 window of it to VGA at (4,4) synchronised to vertical retrace and one timer tick before freeing the buffer.
plate_comment:
Renders and presents one frame of the framed main view.

Algorithm:
1. malloc(0x15180 = 86400) a scratch scene buffer. The buffer is a composite: the first 0x21d8 (8664) bytes are header/state, the pixel plane starts at +0x21d8 and is 360 bytes per scan line.
2. FUN_0002bf60(buf) fills/initialises the buffer (shared helper, 21 callers).
3. FUN_0002dcf0(buf) composes this view's content into it (called from nowhere else).
4. Busy-wait on inp(0x3DA) until bit 3 is set, i.e. until vertical retrace begins.
5. FUN_0002eab0() runs inside the retrace window (4 callers; typical of DAC/palette programming).
6. Busy-wait on inp(0x3DA) until bit 3 clears, i.e. until retrace ends.
7. FUN_0002f2f0(buf + 0x21d8, 0x168, 0xA0504, 0x140, 0x138, 0xC0) blits the composed image to VGA memory: source stride 360, destination 0xA0000 + 0x504 (row 4, column 4 of a 320-wide mode 13h screen), destination stride 320, 312 x 192 pixels. That is exactly the interior of a 4-pixel border around the 320x200 screen.
8. Spin until the interrupt-driven tick counter DAT_00069d64 differs from the last-seen value DAT_00069d10, then latch DAT_00069d10 = DAT_00069d64. This paces the caller to one tick per frame.
9. free(buf) and return.

Parameters: none. Everything drawn is taken from global state, which is why 41 different call sites can invoke it with no arguments.

Returns: nothing.
evidence: Structure is unambiguous from the disassembly: malloc(86400) / free pair around the body (0x3d375 and 0x3d478 are the CRT allocator and deallocator), two inp(0x3DA)-and-test-bit-3 spin loops which is the textbook VGA vertical-retrace wait, and a six-argument blit whose constants decode cleanly as (src, src_stride=360, dst=0xA0504, dst_stride=320, w=312, h=192). 0xA0504 is 0xA0000 + 4*320 + 4, and 312x192 is 320x200 minus an 8-pixel margin, so the destination is the interior of a 4-pixel screen border - a screen-space blit, not a capture. FUN_0002f2f0 has 48 callers including fdps_title_screen and fdps_show_game_over, confirming it is the shared rect-blit-to-screen primitive and that the heap buffer is the source. The trailing DAT_00069d10 / DAT_00069d64 compare-and-latch is a one-tick frame-pacing wait against an interrupt-updated counter. Pool is fdps: it uses only CRT malloc/free/inp plus in-module graphics helpers, and it is called from 41 game-side functions including fdps_battle_player_phase_loop. Prologue 53 56 57 55 89 E5 with 'mov esp,ebp / pop ebp' epilogue and every callee invoked push-args-then-ADD-ESP matches the -4s stack calling convention already established as this binary's default in rebuild_info/build_flags.md, hence __cdecl.
open_question: What is actually drawn is not settled. FUN_0002dcf0 is exclusive to this function, so the content is specific rather than generic, yet the routine takes no arguments and has 41 callers - so the subject comes from globals. Whether callers invoke it once as a repaint or repeatedly as a per-frame loop body (the one-tick wait suggests the latter) is also unresolved. The meaning of the 0x21d8 header region and why the buffer is 360x240 while only 312x192 is shown are unknown. If FUN_0002dcf0 turns out to name the content, this function should be renamed to match it.

name: fdps_draw_scene_layers
role: Advances the scrolling-layer table by one tick and composites its up-to-6 entries into the caller's scene buffer in two depth passes, with the mid-layer content drawn between them.
plate_comment:
Composites the scrolling layer table into a scene buffer.

The layer table is a fixed 6-slot structure-of-arrays block in .data, each array 6 dwords or 6 bytes long and packed back to back: pos_x[6] at 0x69bf0, pos_y[6] at 0x69c08, unknown_a[6] at 0x69c20, vel_y[6] at 0x69c38, vel_x[6] at 0x69c50, scroll_factor_y[6] at 0x69c68, scroll_factor_x[6] at 0x69c80, unknown_b[6] at 0x69c98, image[6] at 0x69cb0, mode[6] (bytes) at 0x69cf8 and depth[6] (bytes) at 0x69cfe. The number of active slots is DAT_00069cdc.

Algorithm:
1. Tick gate: if the interrupt tick counter DAT_00069d64 differs from the last value this function
   latched in DAT_00069d14, add vel_x[i] to pos_x[i] and vel_y[i] to pos_y[i] for every active slot,
   then latch DAT_00069d14 = DAT_00069d64. Position therefore advances once per tick regardless of
   how many times per tick the function is called.
2. FUN_0002c220 fills a local 6-entry array with the slot indices in draw order.
3. Pass one, in that order: for each slot whose depth byte is below 10, compute
   x = (DAT_00069ce4 * scroll_factor_x[i] + pos_x[i]) >> 3 and
   y = (DAT_00069ce0 * scroll_factor_y[i] + pos_y[i]) >> 3 -- a per-slot multiple of the two global
   camera/scroll values plus the slot's own accumulated offset, in 1/8 pixel fixed point -- and call
   FUN_0002c330(buf, image[i], unknown_a[i], DAT_00060144, x, y, unknown_b[i], mode[i]).
4. Draw the mid-layer content into the same buffer: FUN_0002c6a0(buf) then FUN_0002d240(buf, 0).
5. Pass two: the identical loop and blit call for every slot whose depth byte is above 10, so those
   slots land on top of the mid-layer content. Depth exactly 10 is drawn by neither pass.

Parameters:
  buf -- destination scene buffer, passed straight through to every drawing callee.

Returns: nothing.
evidence: The single argument arrives on the stack at [EBP+0x14] (four saved registers plus the return address) and the function returns with a plain RET while every caller adjusts ESP itself, so it is stack-argument, caller-cleaned. It is called from 21 sites, one of which is the already-named fdps_render_view_frame at 0002beb0, which mallocs the 0x15180 scene buffer, calls this function with it, then composes and blits the result to VGA memory -- so the buffer argument and the graphics subsystem are established by the caller. The globals it touches form a clean 6-slot structure-of-arrays table: the dword arrays are exactly 0x18 apart and the two byte arrays are exactly 6 apart (0x69cf8 and 0x69cfe), which fixes the slot count at 6 and identifies the per-slot fields by how each array is used (one pair accumulated by another pair every tick, one pair multiplied by a global before the add, one pair passed as pointer and mode to the blit). The two passes select on the same depth byte with complementary comparisons around 10, with two further draw calls in between, which is a painter's-algorithm layering split. DAT_00069d64 is the interrupt tick counter, already identified in fdps_render_view_frame's plate comment. No CRT or AIL behaviour is present, so the pool is fdps.
open_question: The exact semantics of DAT_00069ce0 / DAT_00069ce4 (read as camera or scroll offsets, making scroll_factor_x/y parallax multipliers) is inferred from the arithmetic shape only, not confirmed at their writers. The three per-slot fields passed straight to FUN_0002c330 (unknown_a at 0x69c20, unknown_b at 0x69c98, and the global DAT_00060144) are unidentified, and it is not established what FUN_0002c6a0 and FUN_0002d240 draw, i.e. what occupies the depth-10 band.

name: fdps_get_unit_record
role: Returns a pointer to element `index` of the heap-allocated global array of 0x50-byte unit records whose base pointer lives at 0x00069cd8.
plate_comment:
Accessor for the global unit-record array.

Algorithm: Multiplies the index argument by the record stride 0x50 (80 bytes) and adds it to the base pointer held in the global at 0x00069cd8, returning the address of that record. No bounds check is performed and the base pointer is not tested for NULL. The array is allocated and filled by fdps_load_savegame, read throughout battle and menu code, and released by fdps_shutdown_free_resources.

Parameters: index - zero-based record index; the caller is responsible for keeping it in range.

Returns: Pointer to the start of the indexed 0x50-byte record. Undefined behaviour if the global base pointer has not been initialised.
evidence: Body is five instructions: IMUL EAX,[EBP+0x14],0x50 / MOV EDX,[0x00069cd8] / ADD EDX,EAX / return EDX - a pure base+index*stride accessor with stride 0x50. The global at 0x00069cd8 is BSS (reads as zero in the image), is WRITTEN in fdps_load_savegame (0x24012) and in FUN_00022be0 / FUN_000232b0, is READ by fdps_battle_player_phase_loop, fdps_battle_unit_turn and dozens of others, and is released in fdps_shutdown_free_resources - i.e. a runtime-allocated array of per-unit records, hence the fdps_ pool and the unit-record name. The accessor itself has 100+ callers spread across the whole game segment (0x10010-0x36f70), which matches a hot data accessor rather than a subsystem entry point. Calling convention: prologue is the canonical Watcom -4s frame 53 56 57 55 89 e5 with the single argument read from [EBP+0x14] and a plain RET (caller cleans), exactly the binary-wide stack convention documented in rebuild_info/build_flags.md, so __cdecl, not __watcall. The decompiler's `int` return and in_stack_00000004 pseudo-parameter confirm the single stack argument; the real return type is a pointer.
open_question: The internal layout and exact meaning of the 0x50-byte record are not established here (party/enemy roster entry vs. battlefield unit slot), so the `unit` in the name is inferred from the writer/reader set rather than from field-level evidence. The array element count is also unknown - it would come from the allocation site inside fdps_load_savegame. Subsystem is tagged battle because the heaviest identified readers are battle functions, but the accessor is called game-wide, not only from battle code.

name: fdps_animate_move_path
role: Walks a byte array of movement step codes and dispatches each step to one of four per-step animation routines, all of which redraw the view frame.
plate_comment:
Plays back a movement path one step at a time.

Algorithm:
Iterates a local counter i from 0 to count-1. For each i it loads the
byte at steps[i] and zero-extends it into a local step code, then
dispatches on that code: 0 calls FUN_0002d360, 1 calls FUN_0002d590,
2 calls FUN_0002d480, and any other value falls through to the default
handler FUN_0002d6a0. Every handler receives the same single argument,
the ctx pointer passed in as the first stack argument; the step byte
itself is not forwarded. All four handlers share the same callee set
(a shared helper pair plus fdps_render_view_frame), so each step code
selects a variant of the same per-step animation-and-redraw work.
The loop body does nothing else; the function has no early exit and no
return value.

Parameters:
ctx    - first stack argument, the animation/actor context handed
         unchanged to every step handler.
steps  - second stack argument, pointer to a byte array of step codes,
         read one byte per iteration.
count  - third stack argument, number of step codes to play back;
         a value <= 0 makes the function a no-op.

Returns:
Nothing. Arguments arrive on the stack and the caller removes them.
prototype: void fdps_animate_move_path(void *ctx, unsigned char *steps, int count)
evidence: Disassembly shows the prologue PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP then MOV EBP,ESP, so the incoming arguments sit at EBP+0x14, EBP+0x18 and EBP+0x1c; no register-passed argument is read anywhere in the body, and the function ends with a bare RET while its own call sites use PUSH EAX / CALL / ADD ESP,0x4. That is stack-passed, caller-cleaned, i.e. __cdecl, not the Watcom default register convention. The body is a plain counted loop: EDX = steps + i, AL = *EDX zero-extended into a local, then a three-way CMP chain on 0/1/2 with a default arm, each arm pushing the same EBP+0x14 argument and calling one of four routines. Pool is fdps because all four handlers call fdps_render_view_frame plus a common helper pair, which is game rendering, not CRT or Miles AIL. Subsystem is battle because one of the two callers is fdps_battle_unit_turn (00015470); combined with a per-step code array and a redraw per step this reads as playing a unit's movement path as an animation.
open_question: The four handlers were not disassembled, so the meaning of step codes 0/1/2/default (most likely movement directions, but possibly animation phases) is unverified, as is the exact type of the ctx argument. The second caller FUN_000119e0 is unnamed, so it is unconfirmed whether this path playback is battle-only or shared with a non-battle map context; if it is shared, the name should lose any battle-specific reading.

name: fdps_map_cursor_move_to
role: Animates the map cursor/focus point from its current pixel position to a target pixel position in tile-sized steps, scrolling the map viewport to keep the cursor inside its margins and redrawing the map whenever the viewport moves.
plate_comment:
Animated move of the map cursor to a target pixel position, with viewport follow.

Algorithm:
Reads the map dimensions from the header pointed to by DAT_00060144 (word[0] = width in tiles, word[1] = height in tiles) and converts them to pixels by multiplying by the 24-pixel tile size. Computes dx = target_x - cursor_x (DAT_00069cd4) and dy = target_y - cursor_y (DAT_00069ccc); returns immediately when both are zero. Picks the axis with the larger absolute delta as the major axis and derives the step count n = abs(major delta) / 24, i.e. one iteration per tile of travel. The major axis advances by (major delta / n) each step; the minor axis uses a running accumulator that adds (acc / n) and carries (acc % n) forward, so the two axes stay proportional without floating point.

After each step the viewport origin is clamped so the cursor stays inside its scroll margins: vertically the cursor must sit between 0x18 and 0x90 pixels below the view top (DAT_00069ce0), horizontally between 0x18 and 0xd8 pixels right of the view left (DAT_00069ce4). When a clamp pushes the view past the map edge it is pulled back to map_pixel_height - 0xc0 or map_pixel_width - 0x138 (the 192x312 visible map window), and negative origins are pinned to 0. A local flag records whether the viewport actually moved; the map is redrawn through FUN_0002beb0 when it moved or when the forced-redraw flag DAT_00069cd0 is non-zero.

Parameters:
  target_x - destination cursor X in pixels (map space, 24 pixels per tile)
  target_y - destination cursor Y in pixels (map space, 24 pixels per tile)

Returns:
  void. Side effects are on the globals: cursor position DAT_00069cd4 / DAT_00069ccc and viewport origin DAT_00069ce4 / DAT_00069ce0.
evidence: Both arguments arrive on the stack at EBP+0x14 and EBP+0x18 (four callee-saved pushes plus the return address) and the function ends with a bare RET, so the caller cleans up: __cdecl, not the Watcom register default. The 0x18 tile size, the map header at DAT_00060144 whose two words are scaled by 0x18 into pixel extents, and the 0x138 x 0xc0 visible window with 0x18 / 0xd8 / 0x90 scroll margins identify DAT_00069cd4 / DAT_00069ccc as a cursor pixel position in map space and DAT_00069ce4 / DAT_00069ce0 as the viewport origin. The only callees are FUN_0003d364, which is a four-instruction abs() (CRT), and FUN_0002beb0, invoked exactly when the viewport moved or the DAT_00069cd0 flag is set, i.e. the map redraw. Nineteen callers, including fdps_battle_player_phase_loop and many event/script routines, match a shared cursor-move helper rather than a one-off. Pool is fdps: game-specific globals, map geometry, no CRT or AIL signature.
open_question: Whether DAT_00069cd4 / DAT_00069ccc is the player-controlled selection cursor or a general camera focus point shared by cutscene panning is not settled from this function alone; the callers would decide it. Subsystem is recorded as graphics because the work done here is viewport scrolling and redraw, but the caller set is dominated by battle-map code.

name: fdps_battle_find_unit_at_cursor
role: Scans the battle unit array for the first unit whose map tile equals the cursor tile and that passes the per-unit predicate at 0x000109b0, returning its index or -1.
plate_comment:
Find the index of the battle unit standing on the cursor tile.

Algorithm:
Iterates i from 0 to the unit count at DAT_00060150, walking the unit array whose base pointer is held in DAT_00069cd8 with a stride of 0x50 bytes per record. For each record it loads the unsigned byte at offset 0 (tile column) and the unsigned byte at offset 1 (tile row) and compares them with the cursor position converted from pixels to tiles: DAT_00069cd4 / 24 and DAT_00069ccc / 24, where 24 (0x18) is the map tile size in pixels. When both coordinates match, it calls FUN_000109b0(i); a return value of zero means the unit qualifies, and the loop stops and returns i. Any mismatch, or a non-zero predicate result, advances to the next record. Falling off the end of the array returns -1.

Parameters:
None. All inputs come from globals: DAT_00069cd8 (unit array base pointer, allocated elsewhere and released by fdps_shutdown_free_resources), DAT_00060150 (unit count), DAT_00069cd4 and DAT_00069ccc (cursor pixel coordinates, moved read-modify-write by fdps_battle_player_phase_loop).

Returns:
The zero-based index of the matching unit, or -1 when no unit on the cursor tile qualifies.
evidence: Standard four-push game-segment prologue with an EBP frame and locals spilled to the stack, matching the -4s -ot -od default; the single call site pushes its argument and cleans up with ADD ESP,4, i.e. the stack calling convention, so __cdecl. The loop bound DAT_00060150 and the 0x50-stride walk over the pointer in DAT_00069cd8 identify a fixed-size record array; DAT_00069cd8 is written by FUN_00023e20 and read by fdps_shutdown_free_resources, so it is an allocated table base, not a scalar. Bytes 0 and 1 of each record are compared against DAT_00069cd4 / 0x18 and DAT_00069ccc / 0x18, a pixel-to-tile conversion with a 24-pixel tile; those two globals are read-modify-written inside fdps_battle_player_phase_loop and read by many draw routines, which is the signature of the on-map cursor rather than a camera origin. Caller set (fdps_battle_player_phase_loop plus five other battle-side routines) and the -1 sentinel return place this in the battle subsystem as an index lookup, hence the fdps_ pool and name.
open_question: Which of DAT_00069cd4 / DAT_00069ccc is the X axis was inferred from record field order (byte 0 = column, byte 1 = row) and not independently confirmed. The meaning of the predicate FUN_000109b0(index), whose zero return makes a unit eligible (most plausibly an alive / on-field / not-hidden test), was not investigated because it lies outside this function.

name: fdps_units_clear_status_bit7
role: Walks every entry of the 0x50-byte battle unit array and clears bit 7 (0x80) of the status byte at unit offset +5.
plate_comment:
Clears status bit 7 (0x80) on every battle unit.

Algorithm: iterates i from 0 while i < the global unit count at 0x00060150. For each i it forms the unit record pointer as (*(char **)0x00069cd8) + i * 0x50, the same base pointer and 0x50 stride used by the battle unit code, and applies AND 0x7f to the byte at unit offset +5, clearing bit 7 while leaving the other status bits intact. No bounds check beyond the count, no early exit, and no other field is touched.

Parameters: none. Both the unit array base pointer and the unit count are read from globals.

Returns: nothing.
evidence: The disassembly is unambiguous: a counted loop over records of stride 0x50 based at the pointer in DAT_00069cd8, bounded by DAT_00060150, applying AND 0x7f to byte +5. Both globals are the battle unit array base and unit count: their other readers include fdps_battle_player_phase_loop, fdps_battle_unit_turn, fdps_battle_find_unit_at_cursor, fdps_battle_map_overview, fdps_battle_end_phase_if_all_units_done, fdps_load_savegame and fdps_load_field_chapter_resources, which places this in the battle subsystem and the fdps pool. The 0x80 bit of unit byte +5 is a genuine one-bit flag: a program-wide instruction search finds it set only at 00010745 (FUN_00010010) and 000119ce (FUN_000119b0), both of which also index the same unit array, and cleared only here and once at 00028bfe (FUN_000288f0). No parameters are taken and no incoming register is read, so the default __watcall applies vacuously; the function is a leaf with no callees. Five callers: FUN_0001e3f0, FUN_00021240, FUN_00021650, fdps_battle_system_menu, fdps_title_demo.
open_question: The meaning of bit 0x80 at unit offset +5 is not settled. It is set per-unit by FUN_00010010 and FUN_000119b0 and bulk-cleared here, which fits a per-phase or per-frame transient flag (acted / highlighted / needs redraw), but nothing in this function distinguishes those. Naming it more specifically requires reading the two setters and the byte +5 readers, which is out of scope for this ticket.

name: fdps_cel_blit_sprite
role: Draws one sprite of a .CEL sheet by index: pulls the sheet-wide width/height from the header, resolves the sprite's RLE stream through the hardcoded offset table at 0x0F, computes the destination address from base + y*pitch + x, and hands all of it to the 13-mode RLE blitter at 0x568db.
plate_comment:
Draw one sprite from a .CEL sheet into a linear 8-bit surface.

Algorithm:
  Reads the sheet-wide sprite size from the .CEL header: signed 16-bit width
  at cel+0x07 and signed 16-bit height at cel+0x09, sign-extended to int.
  Resolves the pixel stream as cel + *(int *)(cel + index * 4 + 0x0F); the
  offset-table position 0x0F is hardcoded, so the header field at 0x05 that
  stores the same value is never read, and neither are the magic, the version,
  the sprite count at 0x0B nor the encoding tag at 0x0D -- there is no format
  validation at all here.
  Computes the destination pointer as dest_base + y * pitch + x, then calls the
  RLE blitter at 0x568db with (stream, dest, width, height, pitch, mode, arg8).
  The blitter is a 13-way dispatch over mode whose variants differ only in
  palette remapping and flipping; the pixel stream format is the 4-op RLE
  described in resource_info/cel.md.
  All arguments arrive on the stack and are read through the EBP frame; the
  callee's seven arguments are cleaned by this function (ADD ESP,0x1C) and this
  function's own arguments are cleaned by its callers, so both sides are cdecl.
  EBX, ESI and EDI are saved and restored but never used.

Parameters:
  cel       pointer to the whole .CEL image loaded in memory (header at offset 0)
  index     zero-based sprite index into the sheet's offset table
  dest_base base of the destination 8-bit surface
  pitch     bytes per destination row
  x         destination column of the sprite's left edge
  y         destination row of the sprite's top edge
  mode      selector forwarded to the blitter's 13-way dispatch (palette remap
            and flip variants)
  arg8      second value forwarded unchanged to the blitter; meaning not settled

Returns:
  Nothing. Draws directly into the caller's surface.
prototype: void fdps_cel_blit_sprite(void *cel, int index, unsigned char *dest_base, int pitch, int x, int y, int mode, int arg8)
evidence: The disassembly matches the .CEL container documented in resource_info/cel.md field for field: MOVSX of word ptr [cel+0x7] and [cel+0x9] as the sheet-wide width and height, and cel + *(int *)(cel + index*4 + 0xf) as the sprite's pixel stream, with the offset-table position 0x0F hardcoded. The single callee 0x568db is the already-identified 13-mode 4-op RLE blitter (mode 0 body at 0x56a0d), the same routine the SAF tile path at 0x13ed0 and the map-tile path at 0x2c330 feed. Destination arithmetic dest_base + y*pitch + x plus the forwarded pitch confirms a linear 8-bit surface blit. 34 callers spread across menu, village, title, battle and field code make it a shared graphics primitive, not a one-off. Convention is cdecl, not the Watcom default: the function reads its first argument from [EBP+0x14] and touches no incoming register, and RET carries no immediate, so the caller pops. Pool is fdps because this is game code operating on a game-specific container, with no CRT or AIL involvement.
open_question: Which of the last two stack arguments is the blitter's mode selector and what the other one carries (a palette remap table pointer or a flip/clip flag) was not settled; the callee at 0x568db was not disassembled under this ticket's read budget.

name: fdps_draw_cursor_info_panel
role: Draws the battle-map information panel for the tile under the cursor: window frame, terrain cel, two text fields, and, when a unit stands there, its animated 24x24 portrait sprite plus current HP.
plate_comment:
Draws the battle-map cursor information panel into the supplied frame buffer.

Algorithm:
1. Computes the cursor position in tile units relative to the scroll origin: col = (DAT_00069cd4 - DAT_00069ce4) / 24, row = (DAT_00069ccc - DAT_00069ce0) / 24 (24 = tile size in pixels).
2. Returns immediately unless both panel-enable flags DAT_00060158 and DAT_00060159 are non-zero.
3. Calls FUN_0002ba00 with the absolute cursor tile (DAT_00069cd4 / 24, DAT_00069ccc / 24) to refresh the data the panel displays.
4. Chooses the panel X origin DAT_0006016c so the panel dodges the cursor: row > 4 and col < 2 selects x = 0x124, row > 4 and col > 10 selects x = 0x19; otherwise the previous value is kept.
5. Blits the panel background cel DAT_000643e0 (width 0xa0) at x, then cel DAT_00069c20 frame DAT_00069d04 (width 0xaf) at x + 9, both into the destination with pitch 0x168.
6. Emits two text fields via FUN_00017530 at byte offsets 0xe6b3 and 0x11d8b (plus x), using the font/colour tables at 0x60040 and 0x60058 indexed by DAT_00069d09.
7. Calls fdps_battle_find_unit_at_cursor. On -1 nothing further is drawn.
8. Otherwise takes the 0x50-byte unit record at DAT_00069cd8 + index * 0x50, derives the walk animation phase from DAT_00069d64 >> 2 & 3 (phase 3 folded back to 1), forms the sprite slot record[2] * 12 + phase, resolves it through the relative offset table at DAT_00060138, and blits the 24x24 sprite at offset 0xf621 + x via FUN_000568db.
9. Sets the text colour global DAT_0006000c to 3 when current HP (record+0x40) differs from max HP (record+0x42), prints the current HP as a 4-digit field at offset 0x10b39 + x, then restores DAT_0006000c to 0.

Parameters:
  dest - destination frame buffer, pitch 0x168 bytes per row; all draw offsets are byte offsets into it.

Returns:
  Nothing.
evidence: Sole caller is fdps_render_view_frame @ 0002beb0 and one callee is the already-identified fdps_battle_find_unit_at_cursor @ 0002daa0, placing this in the battle-map render path. The body reads the cursor position globals, divides by the 24-pixel tile size, and flips the panel X origin between 0x19 and 0x124 depending on whether the cursor sits at the left or right edge of the map view, which is the signature of a floating info window that dodges the cursor. It then blits a background cel plus an overlay cel, draws text with the font tables at 0x60040/0x60058, and for a unit hit indexes a 0x50-byte record array at DAT_00069cd8, animating the sprite with the classic 0-1-2-1 phase fold and printing the record's 16-bit HP field at +0x40 highlighted when it differs from the max at +0x42. All work is game state and drawing, no CRT or AIL behaviour, so the pool is fdps. Convention is __cdecl: the only parameter arrives on the stack at EBP+0x14 (nothing is read from EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX on entry) and every call site here pushes arguments and cleans up with ADD ESP,n.
open_question: The exact meaning of the two text fields drawn at offsets 0xe6b3 and 0x11d8b is unresolved; they are indexed by DAT_00069d09 through the tables at 0x60040 and 0x60058 and are most likely the terrain name and a terrain modifier, but that depends on FUN_0002ba00, which was not read. The role of flags DAT_00060158 / DAT_00060159 and of cel array DAT_00069c20 frame selector DAT_00069d04 is also unconfirmed.

name: fdps_battle_map_overview
role: Shows the whole-battlefield overview: zooms the map out into an off-screen buffer, animates faction-coloured unit markers and a pulsing cursor marker until a key is pressed, then zooms back in and frees its buffers.
plate_comment:
Battlefield overview screen, entered from the player phase.

Algorithm:
1. Allocates a 64000-byte (320x200) off-screen frame buffer and a 0x4000-byte array of 64x64 tile-graphic pointers; calls the minimap tile-graphics loader at 0002e640 for the shared tile source.
2. Reads map dimensions from the map header at DAT_00069cb0 (+7 = width, +9 = height) and the camera pixel origin from DAT_00069ce4 / DAT_00069ce0, converting to tile units by dividing by the 24-pixel tile size. Marker scale defaults to 4 px per tile (virtual width 0x280); maps taller than 40 tiles drop to 3 px per tile (virtual width 0x380).
3. Fills the pointer array: for each tile (x,y) calls the tile lookup at 0002ba00, then takes the resulting tile index from DAT_00069d04 and stores tilesrc + 6 + index * 0x240 (24*24 bytes per tile).
4. Plays a 7-step zoom-out animation: each step interpolates source rect and scale between the camera view and the full map, calls the scaled map blitter at 0002e710 into the off-screen buffer and copies 64000 bytes to 0xa0000.
5. Flushes the keyboard (000567b3) then loops on 000567be until it returns a value <= 0x7f (a real key). Each time the frame counter DAT_00069d64 advances, it redraws all DAT_00060150 units from the unit array at DAT_00069cd8 (stride 0x50): units with bit 0 of byte +5 set are skipped; byte +0 / +1 are tile x / y, byte +6 selects a faction colour base from the table {0x28, 0xb4, 0xd6} copied from 0002b294. A marker square is drawn by 0002e5e0 at (0xa0 + x*scale - width*scale/2, 0x64 + y*scale - height*scale/2). The map cursor (DAT_00069cd4 / DAT_00069ccc divided by 24) is drawn last with colour base 0x82. A shared brightness offset ping-pongs between 0 and 7 each frame, making every marker pulse.
6. Plays the 6-step zoom-in animation in reverse and frees the frame buffer, the pointer array and the tile source.

Parameters: none; all state comes from the battle globals listed above.
Returns: nothing.
evidence: Single caller is fdps_battle_player_phase_loop, so this is a player-phase command. The body allocates a 320x200 (0xfa00) buffer, blits it to 0xa0000 through the memcpy helper 0003d514, and frees through 0003d478 -- classic VGA mode 13h double buffer. The tile-pointer arithmetic (index * 0x240 = 24x24 bytes, array stride 64 entries, camera globals divided by 0x18) matches the game's 24-pixel tile grid. The unit loop walks DAT_00069cd8 with stride 0x50 for DAT_00060150 entries, using byte +6 to index the three-entry colour table at 0002b294 ({40, 180, 214}) -- faction colours for the markers -- and skips units whose byte +5 bit 0 is set. The interpolating 1..7 / 6..1 loops around the scaled blitter 0002e710 are a symmetric zoom-out / zoom-in animation, and the middle wait loop exits on the first key from 000567be. Pool is fdps: game-specific globals, no CRT or Miles signature; the only library calls are malloc/free/memcpy. Prologue 53 56 57 55 89 e5 with 'mov esp,ebp / pop ebp' epilogue and stack-passed, caller-cleaned arguments to every callee is exactly the -4s stack convention recorded in rebuild_info/build_flags.md, hence __cdecl.
open_question: The exact meaning of unit byte +5 bit 0 (assumed 'dead / not on field') and of the flag semantics of 0002ba00's output global DAT_00069d04 were not confirmed from this function alone.

name: fdps_cel_expand_sheet_24x24
role: Allocates a new uncompressed shape buffer and decodes every sprite of the chapter CEL sheet at DAT_00069c20 into it as raw 24x24 cels.
plate_comment:
Expand the whole chapter CEL sheet into a newly allocated uncompressed 24x24 shape array.

Algorithm:
  Takes no arguments; the source sheet is the global CEL pointer at 0x00069c20,
  which is loaded by fdps_load_field_chapter_resources and released by
  fdps_shutdown_free_resources.
  Reads the sheet's sprite count as a signed 16-bit value at cel+0x0B (the same
  field fdps_cel_blit_sprite documents but never reads) and sign-extends it to
  int, then allocates count * 0x240 + 6 bytes through the CRT allocator at
  0x0003d375. 0x240 is 576 = 24 * 24, one byte per pixel, so the sheet's sprites
  are assumed to be 24x24; nothing here validates that against the width/height
  fields in the source header.
  On allocation failure it prints "Out of memory at rease shape !!!" (the typo is
  the original developer's) through the CRT output helper at 0x00042deb and calls
  exit(1) -- the failure path does not return.
  Writes a 6-byte shape header into the new buffer: 16-bit width 0x18, 16-bit
  height 0x18, 16-bit sprite count. Zero-fills the count * 0x240 pixel bytes that
  follow with the CRT memset at 0x00042cd0.
  Then loops i from 0 to count-1 calling
  fdps_cel_blit_sprite(sheet, i, dest_base, 0x18, 6, i * 0x18, 0, 0). The blitter
  computes dest_base + y * pitch + x, so pitch 0x18, x 6 and y i*0x18 resolve to
  dest_base + 6 + i * 0x240 -- x is being abused as a byte fudge to step over the
  6-byte header, not as a real column. Mode 0 means the plain unremapped,
  unflipped RLE variant, so each sprite is written out as a flat 24x24 block.
  Standard four-register prologue (EBX, ESI, EDI, EBP); EBX, ESI and EDI are
  saved and restored but never used. Every callee's arguments are pushed on the
  stack and cleaned by this function (ADD ESP,n), and this function itself takes
  no arguments and ends in a plain RET, matching the module default stack
  convention.

Parameters:
  None. The source sheet is read from the global at 0x00069c20.

Returns:
  Pointer to the newly allocated shape buffer: a 6-byte header (width 24,
  height 24, sprite count) followed by count consecutive 576-byte uncompressed
  24x24 sprites. Never returns NULL -- allocation failure exits the process.
  The caller owns the buffer.
evidence: The disassembly is unambiguous about the mechanism: sprite count from word at [global+0x0B], allocation of count*0x240+6, a 6-byte header written as 0x18/0x18/count, memset of the pixel area, then one fdps_cel_blit_sprite call per sprite. fdps_cel_blit_sprite's settled prototype (cel, index, dest_base, pitch, x, y, mode, arg8) makes the destination address arithmetic resolve exactly to the start of cel i in the new buffer, which fixes the output layout beyond doubt. The failure string "Out of memory at rease shape !!!" at 0x00061E84 confirms the developer's own word for the result is a shape and confirms the CRT pool of the three helpers (malloc, printf-like, exit). Pool fdps: it is game-side image handling, calls only game code plus CRT, and its single caller is fdps_battle_map_overview. Convention __cdecl per rebuild_info/build_flags.md -- the module default is the stack convention, the prologue is the standard four pushes, the function ends in a plain RET, and every call it makes is caller-cleaned.
open_question: Which sheet the global at 0x00069c20 holds is inferred, not proven: it is chapter-scoped (loaded by fdps_load_field_chapter_resources, freed by fdps_shutdown_free_resources) and the only caller is the battle map overview, so terrain tiles are likely, but the global itself is still unnamed. Also unproven is whether the source sprites really are 24x24 -- the 0x18 constants are hardcoded here and the source header's width/height fields are never consulted.

name: fdps_render_map_overview_scaled
role: Renders the scaled battle-map overview by nearest-neighbour sampling 24x24 map tiles through a fixed-point camera into a 312x192 viewport inset at (4,4) of a 320x200 offscreen buffer.
plate_comment:
Renders the scaled (zoomable) battle map overview into an offscreen 320x200 buffer.

Algorithm:
Reads the current map dimensions from the map header pointed to by the global at 0x00069cb0: width = *(int16*)(hdr+7), height = *(int16*)(hdr+9). Converts the requested camera centre into a top-left world position by subtracting step*0x9c horizontally and step*0x60 vertically (0x9c=156 and 0x60=96 are half the 312x192 viewport), so the caller passes the point that should land at the centre of the view.

World coordinates are 1.12-style fixed point with 0xc00 units per map tile and 0x80 units per source pixel, i.e. every tile is 24x24 pixels (0xc00/0x80 = 24). The top-left position is split into tile index (world / 0xc00) and sub-tile remainder (world % 0xc00), with a manual floor correction that adds 0xc00 to the remainder and decrements the tile index when the remainder is negative, so negative camera positions still sample the correct tile.

The destination buffer is first cleared to colour 0 over its full 64000 bytes, then drawing starts at buffer + 0x504 (row 4, column 4) and advances by 0x140 (320) bytes per output row.

For each of 192 output rows the sub-tile Y remainder is converted to a source row offset ((rem >> 7) * 0x18) inside the tile bitmap. Rows whose tile Y is outside [0, height) are skipped, leaving the cleared background. Otherwise the tile bitmap pointer is fetched from the caller-supplied pointer table as table[tileY * 64 + tileX] (the table has a fixed stride of 64 entries per map row) and the row offset is added.

For each of 312 output columns one byte is copied from the tile bitmap at source column (subX >> 7), skipped when tile X is outside [0, width). After each column the sub-tile X remainder advances by step; when it reaches 0xc00 the tile X index advances, the remainder wraps by subtracting 0xc00, and the tile bitmap pointer is re-fetched from the table. The same wrap logic advances tile Y between rows. Tile X and its remainder are restored from the saved row-start values before each new row.

The step parameter is therefore the zoom factor in source-pixel fixed point: 0x80 gives 1:1, larger values zoom out, smaller values zoom in.

Parameters:
  dest       - destination 320x200 8bpp offscreen buffer, cleared to 0 first
  world_x    - camera centre X in 1/0x80-of-a-pixel fixed point (0xc00 per tile)
  world_y    - camera centre Y in the same fixed point
  step       - fixed-point source step per output pixel, i.e. the zoom factor
  tile_table - array of pointers to 24x24 tile bitmaps, indexed [tileY * 64 + tileX]

Returns:
  Nothing. EAX at RET holds the leftover loop counter and carries no meaning.
prototype: void fdps_render_map_overview_scaled(unsigned char *dest, int world_x, int world_y, int step, unsigned char **tile_table)
evidence: All five arguments are read from the stack frame ([EBP+0x14]..[EBP+0x24], the first stack slot being EBP+0x14 after the four entry pushes) and none from EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX; the function ends in a plain RET so the caller cleans up, which is __cdecl, not the register-based __watcall. The only callee (0x00042cd0) is invoked as PUSH 0xfa00 / PUSH 0 / PUSH dest / CALL / ADD ESP,0xc, i.e. memset(dest, 0, 64000) - a CRT helper, so it is not a walk target. 0xfa00 = 320*200 and the 0x140 row stride, 0x504 start offset, 0xc0 row count and 0x138 column count together fix the destination as a 320x200 8bpp buffer with a 312x192 viewport inset at (4,4). The 0xc00 tile unit with >>7 pixel extraction and *0x18 row stride pins tiles at 24x24. The pointer table index (tileY << 6) + tileX gives a 64-entry row stride, and the bounds checks compare tileX against *(int16*)(g_map_hdr+7) and tileY against *(int16*)(g_map_hdr+9), i.e. map width and height. The sole caller is fdps_battle_map_overview at 0002e160, which places this squarely in the battle map overview drawing path, and the multiply-by-step centring plus per-pixel step advance makes it the scaled (zoom) variant. Game rendering logic, no CRT or AIL signature, so pool is fdps.
open_question: The exact zoom values the caller passes for step, and whether the pointer table's fixed 64-entry row stride is a hard map-width cap or just the allocation stride, were not checked (the caller was not read, per the one-function rule).

name: fdps_map_apply_triggered_cell_changes
role: Sweeps every cell of the current map and, for each cell whose kind field marks it as a triggerable object and whose per-cell event flag is already set, advances the cell's tile index by one and clears the matching byte in the second map layer.
plate_comment:
Applies already-triggered map cell state to the tile layer.

Algorithm:
Reads the current map header via the pointer at 0x00069cb0: width = word at +7, height = word at +9; the tile array is a width*height array of 16-bit tile indices starting at +0x0b. Reads a second, parallel map layer via the pointer at 0x00060148: its own width is the word at +7 and its byte array starts at +0x10.
Iterates y over [0,height) and x over [0,width). For each cell it calls the map cell query helper at 0x0002ba00 with (x, y), which publishes the cell record into the globals at 0x00069d00..0x00069d0f; this routine then uses the kind byte at 0x00069d08 and the cell id word at 0x00069d06.
A cell is acted on when (kind & 0x60) equals 0x20 or equals 0x60 and the byte table at 0x000640d8 indexed by the cell id is non-zero. Note that the two equality tests together are exactly the bit test (kind & 0x20), so the original source compared the masked kind against two named constants rather than testing one bit; keep both comparisons when rebuilding.
For an acted-on cell it increments the 16-bit tile index at tiles[y*width + x] by one and stores 0 into the second layer at layer2[y*layer2_width + x].
The table at 0x000640d8 is zero-filled in the image and is passed by address to the savegame reader and writer, so it is persistent per-cell trigger state; this routine is the pass that makes that state visible on the map after a load or a map (re)init.

Parameters:
None. All inputs come from the globals named above.

Returns:
Nothing.
evidence: Disassembly shows no incoming arguments and a pure double loop bounded by the map header width/height at [0x00069cb0]+7/+9, writing 16-bit entries of the tile array at +0x0b and bytes of a second layer at [0x00060148]+0x10. The only callee (0x0002ba00, 15 callers across the program) is the shared map cell query that fills the cell globals at 0x00069d06/0x00069d08, so this is game logic over map data, not CRT or AIL. The gating table at 0x000640d8 is passed as a PARAM by fdps_load_savegame (0x00024062) and by FUN_00022750 (0x00022782), i.e. it is saved and restored state, and this routine is called from fdps_load_savegame plus four map/chapter-level callers, which fits a 'replay persistent map changes onto the tile layer' pass rather than a per-frame update. Name follows the fdps_ snake_case rule for game logic.
open_question: The exact meaning of kind values 0x20 and 0x60 (which object class: chest, door, destructible obstacle) and of the second map layer at 0x00060148 whose byte is cleared (passability, movement cost, or a draw cache) are not settled from this function alone; both would need the writers of 0x000640d8 and the layout of the cell record at 0x00069d00 to pin down.

name: fdps_battle_end_phase_if_all_units_done
role: Scans the battle unit table after a player command and, if no friendly unit is still able to act, calls the phase-completion routine at 0x1E3F0.
plate_comment:
End the player phase once no friendly unit can still act.

Algorithm:
Sets a local 'all done' flag to 1, then walks the battle unit table: index 0 to DAT_00060150-1 (unit count), record base DAT_00069CD8, record stride 0x50 bytes. A record clears the flag when all three of these hold:
  byte +5 (status flags) has neither bit 0x80 nor bit 0x01 set, i.e. the unit is neither already finished nor removed
  byte +6 (side) equals 2, the player's side
  byte +0x26 equals 0, the per-unit acted marker
The loop always runs to completion; it does not break early. Afterwards, if the flag is still 1 -- no friendly unit remains actionable -- it calls FUN_0001E3F0, the phase-completion routine that the battle system menu also invokes after sweeping every remaining unit.

Parameters:
None. The prologue pushes EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP and reserves 0x18 bytes of locals; nothing at [EBP+0x14] or beyond is read, and every local is written before use. The decompiler's param_1/param_2/param_4/unaff_EBX are artifacts, as is the argument list it shows on the call to FUN_0001E3F0 -- the disassembly is a bare CALL with no preceding pushes.

Returns:
Nothing.
evidence: The loop uses exactly the battle unit table already established by the sole caller fdps_battle_player_phase_loop @ 0002BAE0: count at DAT_00060150, base pointer DAT_00069CD8, 0x50-byte records, side byte +6 compared to 2 and flags byte +5 masked, plus the acted marker at +0x26. The caller invokes this routine immediately after the unit command menu (0x15470) returns and only while the phase-end flag 0x69DA0 is still clear, which fixes the purpose as the post-command 'is the phase over?' check. The body has no other effect: the single conditional call to FUN_0001E3F0, whose only other caller is the battle system menu at 0x14AB0 after it forces every remaining friendly unit through its action, confirms 0x1E3F0 is the end-of-phase step rather than a generic helper. Pool is fdps -- it reads game battle state and calls a battle routine; there is no CRT or Miles content. Convention is the module default __cdecl per rebuild_info/build_flags.md: the prologue is the -4s stack-convention shape (PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP; MOV EBP,ESP; MOV ESP,EBP with POPs, no LEAVE) and the function ends in a bare RET with no callee stack cleanup.
open_question: The exact meaning of flags-byte bit 0x01 is inferred (the caller's own scan masks 0x85 while this one masks 0x81, so bit 0x04 is deliberately ignored here); bit 0x80 as 'already acted' and byte +0x26 as a second acted/disabled marker are taken from the caller's tests, not from their writers.

name: fdps_cycle_scene_palette
role: Advances the per-scene VGA palette colour-cycling animation one step each time the frame tick changes, selecting the animated colour ramps by current scene id and writing them to the DAC.
plate_comment:
Advances the VGA palette colour-cycling animation for the current scene.

Algorithm:
1. Copies about twenty short byte ramps out of read-only tables at 0002b2a0..0002b4e9 onto the stack. The ramps come in R/G/B triples; every byte is a 6-bit VGA DAC component (observed range 0..63). Each ramp is (count + count/... ) bytes long so that a sliding window of `count` entries can start at any phase without wrapping: e.g. a 5-colour cycle stores 9 bytes, a 15-colour cycle stores 29 bytes.
2. Calls fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll (00030c50) as per-frame housekeeping.
3. Gates on the frame tick: if the last-serviced tick at 00069d20 already equals the current tick at 00069d64 the function returns without touching the palette, so the animation advances at most once per tick.
4. Switches on the scene / screen id at 00069cf4 (cases 0, 2, 8, 0x14, 0x15, 0x16, 0x17, 0x1a, 0x1c, 0x1d). Each case picks its own R/G/B ramp triple, its own DAC start index (0xf0, 0xf5, 0xf6 or 0xf8) and its own colour count (5, 7, 9, 10, 11 or 15).
5. Advances the shared phase counter at 00069d24 as (phase + 1) mod (count * 4) — the times-four factor makes the cycle advance one colour every four ticks — then derives the window offset as phase / 4 and calls FUN_0002f240(first_index, r + offset, g + offset, b + offset, count) with cdecl argument order (the caller does ADD ESP,0x14).
6. Records the serviced tick by storing 00069d64 into 00069d20.

Unrecognised scene ids fall through to the tick bookkeeping and change no colours.

Parameters: none. All inputs are globals: 00069cf4 scene id, 00069d20 last serviced tick, 00069d24 cycle phase, 00069d64 current frame tick.

Returns: nothing.
evidence: The stack-loaded tables at 0002b2a0+ hold bytes in the 0..63 range arranged as three parallel oscillating ramps per case, which is the VGA 6-bit DAC component range. The single worker FUN_0002f240 spins on FUN_0003d4e4 until bit 8 is set (vertical-retrace poll on the input status register) and then emits four port writes per colour for `count` colours — index, R, G, B — so it is a DAC range write and this function is its only interesting caller pattern. The DAC start indices 0xf0/0xf5/0xf6/0xf8 sit at the top of the 256-entry palette, the conventional place for cycled colours. Ramp lengths match the sliding window exactly in all ten cases (mod value / 4 = colour count, stored bytes = count + count - 1 rounded to the copy size), which rules out any other reading of the phase arithmetic. Callers are frame-level: fdps_render_view_frame (0002beb0) plus three other screen loops, and the tick gate at 00069d20/00069d64 makes it idempotent within a tick. Pool is fdps: game-specific scene ids and game-specific palette slots, no CRT or Miles signature.
open_question: Which concrete screens the scene ids 0, 2, 8, 0x14, 0x15, 0x16, 0x17, 0x1a, 0x1c, 0x1d name, and which on-screen elements own palette slots 0xf0-0xff, are not settled here; that needs the owner of the global at 00069cf4 to be identified.

name: fdps_blit_rect
role: Transfers a rectangular block row by row between two strided buffers, or fills the destination rectangle with a constant byte when the source stride is zero.
plate_comment:
Strided rectangular block transfer for framebuffer/surface memory.

Algorithm:
Two modes selected by src_stride. When src_stride is zero the routine runs in fill mode: it treats src_or_fill as a byte value and calls memset(dst, src_or_fill, bytes_per_row) once per row, advancing dst by dst_stride after each row. When src_stride is non-zero it runs in copy mode: it calls memmove(dst, src, bytes_per_row) once per row, advancing src by src_stride and dst by dst_stride after each row. Both modes loop exactly rows times with a signed comparison, so a rows value of zero or less transfers nothing. No clipping, no bounds check and no transparency test is performed; the caller is responsible for the geometry. The row counter is kept in a stack local and the working src/dst cursors are stack copies of the incoming pointers, so the caller's values are not disturbed.

Parameters:
  src_or_fill  - in copy mode the source base pointer; in fill mode the byte value used to fill every row (only the low 8 bits reach memset)
  src_stride   - bytes added to the source cursor per row; zero selects fill mode
  dst          - destination base pointer
  dst_stride   - bytes added to the destination cursor per row
  bytes_per_row- number of bytes transferred per row
  rows         - number of rows to transfer; signed, values <= 0 do nothing

Returns:
  Nothing.
prototype: void fdps_blit_rect(unsigned int src_or_fill, int src_stride, void *dst, int dst_stride, int bytes_per_row, int rows)
evidence: Disassembly is unambiguous. After PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP and MOV EBP,ESP the return address sits at EBP+0x10, so the six arguments are EBP+0x14 through EBP+0x28; none of EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX is read at entry and the function ends with a bare RET, so all arguments arrive on the stack and the caller cleans them -- __cdecl, not the project default __watcall. The unaff_EBX and the extra parameters in the decompiled C are Ghidra guesses from the wrongly assumed register convention and should be ignored. Both callees were identified from raw bytes rather than by naming them: 0x00042cd0 loads three stack arguments, replicates the low byte of the second across EDX via MOV DH,DL / SHL EDX,8 / MOV DL,DH twice, calls an inner filler and returns the first argument -- a cdecl memset(dst, c, n) wrapper. 0x0003d514 loads three stack arguments, compares src against dst, forms LEA EDX,[ESI+ECX] and compares again to detect overlap, then runs either a forward or an STD backward rep movsd/rep movsb -- a cdecl memmove(dst, src, n). The push order at both call sites (count, then value/src, then dst) matches those signatures exactly, which fixes the meaning of every parameter. The two loop bodies differ only in that the copy branch also advances the source cursor by EBP+0x18, confirming EBP+0x18 is the source stride and that its zero value is what selects the fill path. Pool is fdps: the address is 16-byte aligned like the rest of the game code, it lives well below the CRT region that the two callees sit in, and it is called from 48 sites including the already-identified fdps_title_screen and fdps_show_game_over -- a general-purpose surface rectangle helper for the graphics layer, not a CRT or AIL routine.
open_question: The dual use of the first parameter (pointer in copy mode, byte value in fill mode) means no single C type is honest for it; unsigned int was chosen so neither call style needs a lossy cast. Which of the 48 call sites actually use the fill mode, and therefore whether dst points at the visible framebuffer or at an offscreen surface, was not surveyed -- that requires reading the callers, which is outside this ticket.

name: fdps_transition_random_blocks
role: Reveals a source image onto a destination surface as a mosaic transition, copying block-aligned rectangles in a randomly shuffled order with a delay between passes.
plate_comment:
Mosaic screen transition: copies the source surface to the destination in block-sized rectangles, visiting them in a shuffled order so the image appears in random patches.

Algorithm:
1. Allocates grid_cols*grid_rows entries of 4 bytes (two int16 fields: column, row) via the CRT allocator and fills it with every (col,row) pair of the phase grid.
2. Shuffles the table in place: for every index i it draws two rand() values and forms j = rand()%grid_cols + grid_cols*(rand()%grid_rows), then swaps entry i with entry j. This is a random-swap shuffle, not a Fisher-Yates pass.
3. Computes the block counts: blocks_x = ceil((width/block_w)/grid_cols), blocks_y = ceil((height/block_h)/grid_rows). Each shuffled entry therefore owns a lattice of blocks spaced grid_cols apart.
4. For each shuffled entry (bx,by), walks that lattice. Row index is y = block_h*(j*grid_cols + by); column index is x = bx + i*grid_cols. A block is drawn only when x < width and y < height. Source address is src + y*src_pitch + x*block_w; destination address is dst + y*dst_pitch + (dst_pitch ? x*block_w : 0). Each block is handed to fdps_blit_rect with block_w by block_h.
5. After finishing one shuffled entry it calls the delay/present thunk at 0003d370 with the delay argument, so one entry of the table equals one visible step of the transition.
6. Frees the table before returning.

Note the bound test on the horizontal axis compares a block-column index against the pixel width, while the vertical test compares a pixel row against the pixel height. The horizontal test is therefore far looser than the vertical one; the real bound comes from the blocks_x loop count.

Parameters:
  dst        destination surface base address
  dst_pitch  destination bytes per row; zero suppresses the horizontal destination offset entirely
  src        source surface base address
  src_pitch  source bytes per row
  width      source width in pixels
  height     source height in pixels
  grid_cols  number of phase columns; also the horizontal stride between blocks of one phase
  grid_rows  number of phase rows
  block_w    block width in pixels
  block_h    block height in pixels
  delay      value passed to the per-step delay/present thunk at 0003d370

Returns:
  Nothing.
prototype: void fdps_transition_random_blocks(unsigned char *dst, int dst_pitch, unsigned char *src, int src_pitch, int width, int height, int grid_cols, int grid_rows, int block_w, int block_h, int delay)
evidence: Every argument is read from [EBP+0x14] upward and the function returns with a plain RET, so all eleven arguments arrive on the stack and the caller cleans them: __cdecl, not the Watcom register default. The body is unambiguous from the disassembly: an allocation of grid_cols*grid_rows*4 bytes (0003d375), a nested fill writing two 16-bit fields per entry, a swap loop driven by two calls to the rand helper at 00042cf8, then a triple loop whose innermost action is a six-argument call to the already-identified fdps_blit_rect at 0002f2f0 with (dst+offset, dst_pitch, src+offset, src_pitch, block_w, block_h), a per-entry call to the thunk at 0003d370, and a free at 0003d478. The address arithmetic src + y*src_pitch + x*block_w is textbook surface addressing, and stepping the block lattice by grid_cols while iterating a shuffled table of (col,row) phases is the standard mosaic wipe. Callers are fdps_load_game_screen (00024490) and FUN_000241e0, both screen-presentation sites, which fits a transition effect rather than a general blitter. Pool is fdps: it is game presentation code that calls CRT malloc/free/rand rather than being one of them.
open_question: The horizontal in-bounds test compares a block-column index against the pixel width while the vertical one compares a pixel row against the pixel height; whether this is an original inconsistency or evidence that width is expressed in different units than assumed is unsettled. The exact behaviour of the delay/present thunk at 0003d370 (frame wait, vsync, or timer sleep) and the meaning of the dst_pitch==0 special case were not investigated.

name: fdps_blit_tint_rect
role: Blends one constant palette colour into every pixel of an 8bpp source rectangle at a 0..16 blend weight and writes the resulting palette indices into a destination rectangle.
plate_comment:
Alpha-blends a single constant palette colour over an 8bpp source rectangle.

Algorithm:
blend_table is a [18][256] array of dwords holding each palette entry pre-scaled by a weight, with the three colour channels packed one per byte (channel n in bits 8n+4..8n+7 before the shift below). Rows 0..8 hold weights 0..8; rows 9..17 (dword offset 0x900 = 9*256) hold the complementary weights. To keep the row index inside 0..8 the function folds alpha: for alpha <= 8 the constant colour reads row alpha and the source pixels read row 9+alpha; for alpha > 8 alpha is replaced by 16-alpha, the constant colour reads row 9+alpha' and the source pixels read row alpha'. Either way the constant colour ends up weighted by the caller's alpha and the source pixel by 16-alpha.
The scaled constant colour is fetched once before the loops. For each pixel the scaled source colour is added to it, the sum is shifted right by 4 (dividing out the /16 of the weights) and masked with 0x000F0F0F, leaving 4 bits per channel at bits 0..3, 8..11 and 16..19. Those are folded into a 12-bit index by (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12), giving channel0 in bits 0..3, channel2 in bits 4..7 and channel1 in bits 8..11. That index selects a palette byte from the 4096-entry inverse-palette table rgb444_lut, which is stored to the destination.
Rows advance by src_stride and dst_stride; no clipping, no transparency test, every pixel in the rectangle is written.

Parameters:
src         - source 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
src_stride  - bytes to add to src per row
dst         - destination 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
dst_stride  - bytes to add to dst per row
width       - pixels per row
height      - number of rows
blend_table - base of the [18][256] dword weighted-colour table
rgb444_lut  - base of the 4096-entry packed-RGB to palette-index table
tint_color  - palette index of the constant colour being blended in
alpha       - blend weight of tint_color, 0..16 (0 = source only, 16 = tint only)

Returns:
Nothing.
prototype: void fdps_blit_tint_rect(unsigned char *src, int src_stride, unsigned char *dst, int dst_stride, int width, int height, unsigned int *blend_table, unsigned char *rgb444_lut, int tint_color, int alpha)
evidence: Disassembly is self-contained and leaf (no callees, no globals, no strings): every operand comes from the ten stack parameters at [EBP+0x14]..[EBP+0x38]. The nested loops over [EBP+0x28] rows and [EBP+0x24] columns with per-row additions of [EBP+0x18] to the source pointer and [EBP+0x20] to the destination pointer are an unmistakable rectangle blit. The dword table indexed as base + alpha*0x400 + (index + 0/0x900)*4, the SAR 4 after adding the two entries, the AND 0x0F0F0F and the (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12) fold into a 12-bit value used as a byte index are a textbook 4-4-4 packed-RGB blend followed by an inverse-palette lookup, which places it in the fdps graphics pool rather than crt or ail. The alpha folding at 0003001c (alpha > 8 => alpha = 16 - alpha with the two table halves swapped) shows alpha is a 0..16 weight for the single colour read once at 00030059, i.e. a constant tint rather than a second bitmap. Calling convention: the prologue pushes EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP and never reads EAX, EDX, EBX or ECX before writing them, so no argument arrives in a register as __watcall would require, and the function ends in a plain RET, leaving the caller to clean ten stack arguments.
open_question: The exact channel order inside blend_table and rgb444_lut (which of the three 4-bit fields is R, G and B) cannot be settled from this function alone; it is fixed by whoever builds those tables. Whether the two callers use it for a screen-wide fade or for a smaller sprite-sized region is likewise not visible here.

name: fdps_audio_init
role: Brings up the Miles AIL sound system: starts the library, installs the MDI (music) and DIG (digital) drivers, allocates one sequence handle and eight sample handles into the global audio state, then hands its argument on to the follow-up audio setup routine at 000307b0.
plate_comment:
Audio subsystem bring-up.

Algorithm:
1. Call AIL startup (0003d718) unconditionally.
2. Clear the two driver-present flags (0x00069d72, 0x00069d71) and set the audio-enabled flag 0x00069d70 to 1.
3. Install the MDI/music driver (0004044c) and store the driver pointer in 0x00069d6c. If it is non-NULL, set flag 0x00069d72 and allocate a single sequence handle (0004067d) into 0x00069d60.
4. Install the DIG/digital driver (0003ea65) and store the driver pointer in 0x00069d68. If it is non-NULL, set flag 0x00069d71 and allocate eight sample handles (0003ecaa) into the array at 0x00069d30.
5. Tail-call the follow-up audio setup routine 000307b0, forwarding this function's single argument.

Both driver installs are optional: a NULL return leaves the corresponding flag at 0 and the game runs without that half of the audio system. The loop counter body contains a dead load of the index, which is normal for the -4s / unoptimised build.

Parameters:
  param1 - opaque value forwarded unchanged to 000307b0; not inspected here.

Returns:
  void.
evidence: Disassembly shows the exact -4s prologue documented in rebuild_info/build_flags.md (PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP; MOV EBP,ESP) with the single argument at [EBP+0x14] and a MOV ESP,EBP / POP / RET epilogue with no callee stack cleanup, so the function is stack-convention (__cdecl) game code, not library code. Its five callees all live in the 0x3d000-0x44000 linked-in Miles AIL region (0004044c wraps its body in the AIL nesting-depth trace log at 0x00069e6c and calls the AIL log helper 00045183), and the call shape is the textbook Miles sequence: AIL_startup, install MDI driver -> allocate exactly one sequence handle, install DIG driver -> allocate exactly eight sample handles into an 8-entry global array at 0x00069d30. The globals written (three byte flags, two driver pointers, one sequence handle, eight sample handles) are the game's own audio state block, which places the function itself in the fdps pool. Callers are main (00029220) and 00030f40, consistent with a startup-time subsystem entry point.
open_question: The meaning of the single argument is not determined here: it is only forwarded to 000307b0, whose body was not examined. Which of 0x00069d72 / 0x00069d71 is music vs. digital is inferred from the handle counts (1 sequence vs. 8 samples) rather than proven, and the purpose of the unconditional flag 0x00069d70 = 1 is unconfirmed.

name: fdps_audio_shutdown
role: Shuts the audio subsystem down at exit by calling AIL_shutdown, the counterpart to fdps_audio_init.
plate_comment:
Tear down the Miles AIL audio stack on the way out of the game.

Algorithm:
  The entire body is the Watcom four-push prologue, a single call to
  AIL_shutdown (0003d8b2), and the matching epilogue. Nothing else: no
  argument is passed, no global is touched, no return value is inspected.

  Identity rests on three things rather than on anything the body itself
  says. The callee at 0003d8b2 is the Miles public API entry AIL_shutdown,
  fixed by the string "AIL_shutdown()\n" at 000623a5 and the standard Miles
  log-wrapper shape around it. This function is the second step of main's
  three-call teardown sequence, between fdps_shutdown_free_resources
  (00029440) and fdps_cd_stop_audio (0003c4a7). And it is the exact
  counterpart of fdps_audio_init (000304e0), which is the one-time AIL
  startup called from main's init sequence.

  A wrapper this thin exists because the game calls AIL through its own
  one-per-operation shims rather than calling the library directly; the same
  pattern appears throughout the audio subsystem.

Parameters:
  None. No register is read before being written and no stack slot is
  accessed.

Returns:
  Nothing. AIL_shutdown's result, if any, is discarded.
evidence: Body is 12 instructions: PUSH EBX/ESI/EDI/EBP, MOV EBP,ESP, SUB ESP,0, CALL 0003d8b2, POP EBP/EDI/ESI/EBX, RET. The verdict for 0003d8b2 identifies it as AIL_shutdown at high confidence, on the strength of the "AIL_shutdown()\n" string at 000623a5 sitting inside the block of Miles API name strings, plus the textbook Miles wrapper body. main (00029220) calls 00029440, then this function, then 0003c4a7, which is the release-resources / stop-audio / stop-CD teardown triple. fdps_audio_init (000304e0) is the symmetric AIL startup on the init side.
_supersedes: The first reading of this function returned low confidence and the placeholder name fdps_unknown_000305a0, correctly, because nothing in the body identifies it: its meaning is entirely its callee's meaning. The callee was walked in a later round, which settled it. Recorded here because the workflow has no mechanism to feed a later round's findings back into an earlier round's verdict.

name: fdps_timer_tick_handler
role: Periodic timer callback installed by fdps_audio_timer_install that bumps the global tick counter and then runs the per-tick service routine at 00042cf8.
plate_comment:
Periodic timer tick callback.

Algorithm: Increments the global 32-bit tick counter at 00069d64, then calls the per-tick service routine FUN_00042cf8 and returns. The tick counter is read (never written) by roughly fifty game functions -- title screen, game over, view rendering, and many battle/menu routines -- which sample it to build delay and frame-pacing loops, so this handler is the single writer that makes those loops advance. The function's address is taken and passed to fdps_audio_timer_install (address reference at 000307bc, stored at 000307c1), which is the only reference to it: nothing calls it directly, it is invoked from the installed timer hook. The body touches no parameters and no registers beyond the standard PUSH ESI/EDI/EBP frame; the SUB ESP,0x0 is Watcom's empty-locals prologue.

Parameters: None.

Returns: Nothing.
evidence: Only reference to 00030790 is as an address operand inside fdps_audio_timer_install (PARAM at 000307bc, DATA at 000307c1) and there are zero call sites, which is the signature of an installed timer callback rather than an ordinary routine. The body is two statements: INC dword ptr [00069d64] and CALL 00042cf8. 00069d64 has ~50 READ-only cross references spread across title screen, game over, rendering and battle code and no other writer, so it is the free-running tick counter and this handler is what advances it. Everything is game code in the 0x30000 text range reached from the game's own audio timer installer, so pool fdps; subsystem audio follows from the installer's established name.
open_question: What FUN_00042cf8 actually services is not established here -- it is called by this ISR plus 18 ordinary game functions, so it may be a music/sound poll that game code also pumps during long operations, or a more general per-frame service. Whether the subsystem label should be audio or a general timing/system label depends on that answer.

name: fdps_audio_timer_install
role: Registers the audio tick callback at 0x00030790 with the timer service, aborts with " Timer fail !!!" if registration fails, programs the timer with the caller-supplied rate and starts it.
plate_comment:
Installs and starts the audio service timer.

Algorithm:
  1. Calls the timer-registration routine FUN_0003e196 with the address of the
     tick callback FUN_00030790 (which bumps the counter at 0x00069d64 and then
     calls the audio service routine FUN_00042cf8). The returned timer handle is
     stored in the global at 0x00069d50.
  2. If the handle is -1 the registration failed; the fatal/report routine
     FUN_00042deb is called with the literal " Timer fail !!!\n" at 0x00061ea8.
     Execution is not stopped locally - the function falls through regardless.
  3. Calls FUN_0003e3ea(handle, rate) to program the timer with the rate value
     passed in by the caller.
  4. Calls FUN_0003e5b3(handle) to start the timer.

All three timer routines are reached with arguments pushed on the stack and the
caller cleaning up (ADD ESP,n after each CALL), i.e. the vendor sound library's
stack convention.

Parameters:
  rate - timer rate/period value handed straight to the timer programming call;
         the only stack slot this function reads ([EBP+0x14]).

Returns:
  Nothing. The timer handle is left in the global at 0x00069d50 for later use.
evidence: Single caller is fdps_audio_init @ 000304e0, which places this squarely in the audio subsystem. The body is the textbook register/check/set-rate/start timer sequence: a function pointer (0x00030790, a two-statement ISR that increments the tick counter DAT_00069d64 and calls FUN_00042cf8) is handed to FUN_0003e196, the returned handle is stored in DAT_00069d50 and compared against -1, and on failure the string at 0x00061ea8 - " Timer fail !!!\n", confirmed by reading memory - is passed to the reporting routine FUN_00042deb. The handle is then passed with the caller's argument to FUN_0003e3ea and alone to FUN_0003e5b3.
